synopsis: Labels are a distinct simulation layer, not a by-product of visual realism: their ontology must follow safety requirements, and useful truth channels extend to geometry, trajectories, visibility, machine state and braking-related quantities [f86, f3979, f3978]. The recommended ground-truth approach combines surveyed targets, reference lidar with RTK-GNSS/INS and audited automatic labels, with an explicit “truth unavailable or ambiguous” state for dust, occlusion and reference-sensor failure [f5197, f5394]. Automatic labeling offers scale, but on-road successes do not establish validity near heavy off-road equipment; one 2026 labeler achieved recall of 0.88–0.98 but precision of only 0.52 in crowded indoor scenes, supporting pre-labeling with stratified human audits rather than an unaudited safety oracle [f5199, f5200, f5382, f5383]. Procedural simulation can supply automatically generated, nominally perfect labels, but this does not resolve whether those labels represent the safety-relevant categories and states [f3975, f4295, f3979]. For a team starting in October 2026, a labeled replay pipeline is considered realistic by mid-2027 only if suitable data exist; the indicative plan starts 180 days of labeling and replay work on January 1, 2027, while current retention of suitable logs and labels remains unestablished [f837, f898, f519]. Labeling is expected to dominate replay costs and may be its real bottleneck, yet project cost figures were not found, so a small representative annotation trial is recommended before budgeting at scale [f522, f1144, f10828, f10829].
